docs.title: JKLab
docs.text:
Warehouse of Public Key Infrastruct JKLab.

JKLab is a technology development brand dedicated to researching PKI and cryptographic technologies and creating practical software tools. Leveraging expertise in certificates, digital signatures, encryption, and security protocols, we aim to resolve technical challenges faced by developers and provide efficient development environments. We continuously research and develop PKI development tools and cryptography-related solutions, including our flagship project, BerEditor. By bridging specialized technology with practical tools, JKLab supports the development of security software that is both more convenient and efficient.

Features PKI Technology

PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is a security framework that utilizes public-key cryptography to verify the identities of users and systems, while ensuring data confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. It serves as a core foundational technology for internet communication, digital signatures, digital certificate management, and corporate security systems.

BerEditor

BerEditor is an integrated GUI tool designed to support developers working with PKI and cryptographic technologies. It facilitates the development of security protocols and troubleshooting by analyzing and validating ASN.1 encoded data, digital certificates, digital signatures, and various other PKI-related data.

CertMan

CertMan is a certificate management tool that supports the management and verification of digital certificates and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). It enables users to examine certificate issuance details, validity periods, public keys, extension fields, and certificate chains, while facilitating the efficient execution of technical tasks related to certificate management.

CryptokiMan

CryptokiMan is a tool designed to support the management and development of cryptographic devices and tokens based on the PKCS#11 standard. It interfaces with Hardware Security Modules (HSMs), smart cards, and PKCS#11-compliant cryptographic modules, enabling users to verify and test cryptographic objects, key pairs, cryptographic operations, and digital signature functions.

docs.title: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI): Concepts
docs.text:
PKI / General Information · April 27, 2023

The term PKI appears in many fields. After working with it for a long time, I have come to think of PKI as a component that supports many different systems. It is rarely used on its own, but it turns up in many places. This article offers a brief overview of the concept.

docs.title: 1. What is PKI?
docs.text:
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is a system of capabilities, policies, and services that uses public-key cryptography to support authentication of users and devices.

There is no single universally fixed list of PKI components. A typical PKI includes Certificate Authorities (CAs) and Registration Authorities (RAs), and uses certificates issued by a CA to authenticate users or devices. The certificate and its issuing authority distinguish PKI from a generic public-key cryptography system.

docs.title: 2. PKI components
docs.text: The diagram below shows common PKI components and their relationships.

docs.title: 2.1 Certificate Authority (CA)
docs.text:
• Issues and distributes certificates for entities such as other CAs and end entities.
  • Revokes certificates at the request of an RA or a user, according to the PKI's procedures.
  • Publishes Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) in a public location, often a directory service (DS).

docs.title: 2.2 Registration Authority (RA)
docs.text:
• Identifies users and asks a CA to register them or issue certificates.
  • Can request certificate revocation and provide certificate status lookup services.

docs.title: 2.3 Directory Server (DS)
docs.text:
• Stores and publicly publishes certificates and CRLs so they can be retrieved by others.
  • Often uses LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol).
  • May also publish information through web or FTP services.

docs.title: 2.4 End Entity (EE)
docs.text:
• A user, device, or other subject that uses a certificate issued by a CA.
  • May create digital signatures or verify signatures, depending on its role.

docs.title: 3. Additional PKI services
docs.text: A PKI can operate with its core components, but additional services can provide useful security and status information.

docs.title: 3.1 Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
docs.text:
• CRLs are published periodically, so they may not reflect a certificate's status immediately.
  • A CRL can also be large and require significant network traffic. OCSP can return status information for an individual certificate.
  • OCSP is commonly used as an alternative or complement to retrieving a full CRL. The actual freshness of a response depends on the service and its configuration.

docs.title: 3.2 Time-Stamping Authority (TSA)
docs.text:
• A TSA provides trusted evidence that data existed at a particular time.
  • It responds to a time-stamp request with a signed token that binds a time to a digest of the submitted data.
  • Time-stamp services can also provide ordering information, such as a sequence number, when the service is designed to do so.

docs.title: 4. PKI use cases
docs.text: PKI supports many kinds of systems. Common examples include:

docs.title: 4.1 Web security
docs.text: • TLS certificates are used to authenticate servers in HTTPS connections and support secure communication.

docs.title: 4.2 Document encryption and signatures
docs.text: • Certificates can be used in workflows for encrypting documents such as PDFs and for creating or verifying digital signatures.

docs.title: 4.3 Email authentication and encryption
docs.text:
• S/MIME uses certificates for signing and encrypting email.
  • OpenPGP (often called PGP) is also based on public-key cryptography, but its key distribution and trust models are not inherently based on the X.509 certificate hierarchy used by many PKI systems.

docs.title: 4.4 User authentication
docs.text: • Certificate-based technologies are used for user authentication, including in some VPN deployments.

docs.title: 4.5 Online banking
docs.text: • In South Korea, PKI systems have been used in various online banking services to authenticate users.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
PKI brings together many technologies: each component and each certificate-related process has its own details. This article has covered only the basic concepts, as a starting point for understanding the wider system.

Tags: DS · EE · certificates · CA · RA · PKI · Public Key Infrastructure · End Entity

docs.title: A Story About Digital Signatures and Certificates
docs.text:
PKI / General Information · May 3, 2023

Digital signatures and certificates are technical topics in public key infrastructure (PKI). Here is a plain-language explanation.

docs.title: The seal certificate analogy
docs.text:
A useful real-world analogy for a digital signature and a certificate is a certificate of registered seal. In a paper-based process, someone signs a document with a seal, and the certificate helps others confirm that the seal is valid and belongs to that person.

In the offline world, people handle identity checks and documents in person. As these processes move online, they are digitized: a person signs data with a private key, and another party verifies the signature with the corresponding public key. A certificate is a digitally signed document that vouches for the relationship between that public key and its subject.

The analogy is not exact, but it helps explain the roles. A seal is applied to a physical document. A digital signature is computed over digital data, so changing the data after signing causes signature verification to fail. In a paper process, people may compare a copy with the signed original to check whether the document was altered.

docs.title: Security needs when moving online
docs.text:
When paper-based processes move online, we need to consider several security properties:

  1. Confidentiality — Only authorized people should be able to read the document.
  2. Integrity — Changes to the digital data should be detectable.
  3. Authenticity — The recipient should be able to verify who signed the document.
  4. Non-repudiation — The signature can provide evidence that the holder of the signing key signed the data, making a later denial harder.

In an offline process, identity documents can help establish who is present; an envelope can limit who sees the contents; and comparing copies can reveal changes. A person also signs the document directly. Online, cryptography helps address these needs: digital signatures provide integrity checks and support signer authentication and non-repudiation, while encryption protects confidentiality.

docs.title: Why certificates matter
docs.text:
Anyone can generate a key pair for creating digital signatures. But how can a verifier know that a particular public key belongs to the person it claims to represent?

A trusted party must vouch for that association. The digitally signed statement that binds a public key to its subject is a certificate. A certificate does not prove that a document is safe or that every claim in it is true; it helps establish trust in the identity associated with a public key.

People can also own more than one physical seal. A certificate of registered seal helps distinguish the seal officially associated with a person. Digital certificates play a related role for public keys.

We trust a certificate of registered seal because it is issued by an authorized public institution. Digital certificates are issued by a Certificate Authority (CA), so trust in the CA matters. Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the set of policies, roles, systems, and processes that supports issuing, managing, and validating certificates and public keys.

docs.title: In summary
docs.text:
As society moves from offline processes to digital ones, we need security mechanisms suited to digital data. Encryption helps provide confidentiality, and digital signatures help protect integrity and establish the signer’s identity. PKI provides an infrastructure for trusting the public keys used in these online interactions.

Tags: certificates · CA · registered seals · PKI · digital signatures

docs.title: Private Keys, Public Keys, and Certificates
docs.text:
PKI / General Information · January 24, 2024

When you work with a PKI system, you often encounter three terms: private key, public key, and certificate. They are fundamental to digital signatures. Here is a simple explanation.

In short:

  • The private key creates a digital signature.
  • The public key verifies that signature.
  • A certificate vouches for the identity associated with a public key.

For an introduction to digital signatures and certificates, see A Story About Digital Signatures and Certificates.

docs.title: What is a private key?
docs.text:
A private key is used to create a digital signature. It must remain under the control of its owner and must not be shared with other people. Protecting the private key is one of the central security requirements of a PKI system.

Private keys are therefore often stored in encrypted form or protected by a more secure device, such as a Hardware Security Module (HSM).

docs.title: What is a public key?
docs.text:
A public key is used to verify a digital signature. The person who holds the private key creates the signature; anyone who needs to check the signed content can use the corresponding public key to verify it.

Signature verification normally uses both the signature and the original data. A digital signature by itself does not provide confidentiality. It lets a verifier check that the signed data has not changed and that the signature was made by someone with the corresponding private key.

As its name suggests, a public key is intended to be shared so others can verify signatures. Unlike a private key, it generally does not need to be kept secret.

docs.title: What is a certificate?
docs.text:
Anyone can generate a public and private key pair. That means anyone can create signatures and anyone can verify a signature if they have the corresponding public key. The remaining question is: whose public key is it?

A certificate helps answer that question. A Certificate Authority (CA) issues a certificate that binds a subject’s identity to a public key. The CA signs the certificate data with its private key. A verifier can use the CA’s public key to check that signature and determine whether the certificate was signed by that CA and whether its contents have been altered.

A CA typically issues certificates and makes them available through a public repository or other distribution service. Because a certificate contains the public key, people can obtain the key from the certificate and use it to verify signatures.

docs.title: In summary
docs.text:
The basic idea of signature verification in a PKI system is straightforward: the private key signs, and the public key verifies. Validating a certificate involves more steps. A verifier may need to build and validate a certificate path through intermediate CAs up to a trusted root, and check that the certificates are valid for the intended use. This process is called path validation.

Understanding these basic terms is a useful first step toward understanding the more complex parts of PKI.
